result.summary: The Chorus fears the curse of Oedipus, and a Messenger reports that Thebes is safe but Eteocles and Polynices have killed each other. Antigone and Ismene lament over the bodies, and a Herald announces that Polynices must lie unburied; Antigone defies the decree, and the Chorus splits to follow each brother.

scenes.title: Chorus fears the family curse
scenes.summary: The Chorus recalls the sin of Laïus, the fate of Oedipus and his curse on his sons, and fears its fulfilment.
scenes.stakes: The city and the royal house may fall to the curse of Oedipus.

scenes.title: Messenger reports the brothers dead
scenes.summary: The Messenger says the city is saved at its gates, but the sons of Oedipus have slain each other.
scenes.stakes: The city's safety is bought with the lives of its two princes.

scenes.title: Chorus mourns as bodies arrive
scenes.summary: The bodies are brought in, and the Chorus laments the brothers and the curse that destroyed them.
scenes.stakes: The race of Oedipus is wholly destroyed.

scenes.title: Antigone and Ismene's dirge
scenes.summary: The sisters chant a dirge over their dead brothers, with the Chorus responding.
scenes.stakes: The sisters face the loss of both brothers and the ruin of their house.

scenes.title: The decree and Antigone's defiance
scenes.summary: A Herald forbids burial of Polynices; Antigone vows to bury him anyway, and the Chorus divides.
scenes.stakes: Antigone risks punishment by the State for burying her brother.

alias_notes.explanation: The Avenging Spirit is the personified curse of Oedipus on his sons, not Oedipus himself.
Thebans are called Cadmean after Cadmus, the city's founder.

notable_quotes.reason: Antigone's memorable line that strife is slowest to end disputes.
Antigone's defiance of the State, anticipating Sophocles' Antigone.

analysis.text: Inherited guilt and the fulfilment of curses drive the fall of the house of Laïus, while the city survives.
The Antigone scene is often thought to be a later addition, and it sets burial duty against state decree.

legacy.text: Antigone's defiance of the burial ban was developed by Sophocles in his play Antigone.

fun_facts.text: Many scholars think the final Antigone and Herald scene was added after Aeschylus, to link the play to Sophocles' Antigone.

language_notes.text: "Avenging Spirit" translates the Erinys (Fury), here the embodied curse of Oedipus; "bringeth" and "forebodeth" are archaic verb endings.
The "stranger" is iron (steel), named from the Chalybes of Scythia, famed metalworkers. It will divide the inheritance by the sword, giving each only a grave.
Pytho is Delphi, regarded as the earth's centre. Apollo's oracle warned Laïus that having a son would cause his death.
The "hallowed field" is Jocasta's womb; Oedipus sowed seed where he himself was nurtured. "Growth of blood" means his children, born of incest.
Refers to throwing cargo overboard in a storm to save the ship; prosperity, when excessive, is sacrificed in disaster.
The "deadly pest" is the Sphinx, whom Oedipus defeated by solving her riddle, saving Thebes.
"Malisons" means curses; "tendance" means treatment or care, here the sons' insulting treatment of their blinded father.
"Mother-bred children" addresses the Theban women of the Chorus as children of the motherland, their native city.
Apollo, guardian of the seventh gate, is said to have taken the brothers there; Laïus had defied his warning not to beget a son, and the curse followed.
"Commander of Sevens": Apollo was associated with the number seven, and the seventh day was sacred to him.
The Chorus calls itself a prophetess of ill because its earlier fears of disaster have proved true.
"Hammered steel of Scythia" means swords made of iron from the Chalybes, a people of the Black Sea region; the "portioned wealth" is the brothers' inheritance.
The father's curse: Oedipus cursed his sons, praying they would divide their inheritance by the sword.
Polynices means 'man of much strife' in Greek; the Chorus plays on the meaning of the name, which fits his fate.
The 'Song of the Spear' is the curse of Oedipus, which foretold his sons would divide their inheritance by the sword.
Acheron is a river of the underworld; the 'sable-sailed mission-ship' is the ferry carrying the dead to Hades.
'Clasp their girdle about their robes' is a periphrasis for 'women'.
Ironic riddle: the portion awaiting them is only burial space, as much earth as a tomb holds.
The 'stranger from beyond the sea' is iron, the sword. Iron was imagined as coming from a foreign land (the Chalybes).
Bitter paradox: their only 'wealth' is the earth of their graves.
"Smitten, thou didst smite" addresses a dead brother: each wounded the other in their duel at the seventh gate.
"Anigh" is archaic for "near"; the sisters say these two sorrows (the brothers' deaths) are closely bound together.
"Kindred unto kindred" stresses that kin killed kin, so the grief is doubled within one family.
Refers to Oedipus's curse, which doomed his sons to divide their inheritance by the sword; the Spirit of Vengeance is the Erinys that fulfils it.
"Hes" is a misprint in the source for "his" or "her"; the line means he took away another's life as he lost his own.
"Threefold woes" refers to the curse on Oedipus's line: the father's fate and the two brothers' mutual slaughter.
Oedipus's curse that his sons would divide their inheritance by the sword is the "Spirit of Vengeance" fulfilled in their deaths.
"To face him with thy spear" refers to Eteocles's brother Polynices returning from exile to attack Thebes, meeting Eteocles in combat.
"Possessed of an evil spirit" means driven by a malignant divine power, here the family curse, to their ruin.
Their father Oedipus is buried nearby; burying the brothers beside him is said to add to his sorrow.
"Cadmus" is the legendary founder of Thebes; "Cadmean" simply means Theban. "Hath in charge" means has responsibility for.
"Were it not that" means he would have destroyed the land except that a god, working through Eteocles' spear, stopped him.
"Guerdon" means reward or recompense, used here bitterly; "barrow" is a burial mound.
"Yea" is an archaic "yes"; Antigone answers the Herald's decree by defiantly addressing the rulers directly.
Burying a body by scattering earth was a minimal rite; Greeks believed the unburied dead could not find rest.
Antigone means that strife (enmity) is the last of the gods to end a quarrel; her hostility to the decree will not yield, and the line is cryptic.
"Own-will" means your own stubborn choice; the Herald washes his hands of her but repeats the ban.
The Vengeful Spirits are the Furies (Erinyes), here embodying the curse of Oedipus that destroyed his sons Eteocles and Polynices.
"Adread" is archaic for afraid; "townsfolk" are the citizens who enforce the decree.
Refers to Eteocles, who died defending Thebes (the Cadmean realm, named for founder Cadmus) against the invading Argive army.

context_notes.text: The Chorus is a group of Theban women, terrified as the city is besieged by seven attacking champions.
On learning he had killed his father and married his mother, Oedipus blinded himself with brooches from Jocasta's dress.
The Messenger is a Theban scout or soldier who brings news from the seven gates after the battle.
The sons of Oedipus, Eteocles and Polynices, killed each other at the seventh gate, one defending Thebes and one attacking it.
Cadmus founded Thebes. The Chorus are Theban women who feared the city's fall during the siege.
Antigone and Ismene are the sisters of the dead brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, and daughters of Oedipus.
Their mother Jocasta unknowingly married her own son Oedipus, so the brothers were also his sons and her grandsons-by-incest.
Eteocles and Polynices, sons of Oedipus, killed each other in single combat over rule of Thebes. Their sisters mourn beside their biers.
The Chorus of Theban maidens blames Fate and the family curse, a central theme of the trilogy about the house of Laius.
Antigone and Ismene are the sisters of the dead brothers Eteocles and Polynices. They sing the lament in alternating lines.
Oedipus, former king of Thebes, cursed his sons Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other in battle at the city's gates.
Polynices led the Argive army against Thebes, his native city, and he and his brother Eteocles killed each other in single combat.
Antigone and Ismene are sisters of both dead brothers. Some scholars think this final scene was added to Aeschylus' play later.
The Herald speaks for Thebes: Polynices led a foreign army against his own city, so the State denies him burial as a traitor.
Greek custom made burial and mourning by kin a sacred duty; denying them was a grave dishonour.
The Chorus splits into two halves, one siding with Antigone and burying Polynices, the other escorting Eteocles.

literary_notes.text: Steel is personified as a foreign settler and ruthless land-divider, grimly recasting the brothers' inheritance as burial plots.
Troubles are waves and Thebes a ship; the third crest evokes the third generation of the cursed house.
The Chorus's dread of the curse's fulfilment anticipates the brothers' mutual death.
The city is a ship that has weathered the storm of war without taking in water, an image of safety under pressure.
The Messenger breaks off mid-sentence, delaying the news and heightening the Chorus's dread.
The brothers' inheritance is the grave plot they share. Dividing the wealth with steel turns the curse into a grim literal fulfilment.
The Chorus addresses the curse directly as if it were a present being, stressing its fulfilment.
'Twofold' and 'double' repeat to mirror the paired brothers and paired deaths.
The brothers finally divide their inheritance equally, but only as graves, mocking their quarrel over the property.
Steel is called a 'stranger' and 'resolver', and Ares an 'apportioner', making war an agent of the curse.
The Curses sing a victory song like a triumphant army, as the family is routed.
Ismene answers Antigone line by line, reversing the verbs (smite/slain). This mirrors the brothers' mutual killing.
The matching phrases "lament be poured forth" and "tears be poured forth" give the dirge a ritual, liturgical rhythm.
The Chorus addresses Fate and the Shade of Oedipus directly, treating the curse as a living, powerful being.
Saved yet lost: the city's survival is bought with the brothers' deaths, a contradiction that sums up the tragedy.
The sisters answer each other line by line in short exclamations, giving the dirge a ritual, echoing rhythm of shared grief.
The Chorus addresses Fate and Oedipus's Shade directly, treating the curse as a living power that has fulfilled itself.
She exclaims at the power of kinship, then addresses her own soul in the next line, voicing inner resolve.
Antigone mocks the word "decree" by quoting it scornfully, rejecting the state's authority over family duty.
Her calm appeal to divine law over human decree shows Antigone's firm, pious defiance in few words.
Strife is imagined as a god who is stubbornly last to end any quarrel, giving Antigone's defiance a divine weight.
The Chorus's rapid questions in sentences 260–262 convey anguish and indecision as it faces a conflict between fear and duty.
The half-chorus shows that civic law is changeable while kinship bonds endure, setting family loyalty against State authority.
